5 Apple Watch settings that can help you save its battery life

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A few changes can help give your Apple Watch extra hours of battery when you need it all day.
  • Recent findings suggest that among the improvements the Apple Watch receives with each iteration, battery life is something everyone wants more of.
  • If your Apple Watch's battery health has depleted significantly, bringing it in for a battery replacement could help restore its original endurance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few changes can help give your Apple Watch extra hours of battery when you need it all day.

Recent findings suggest that among the improvements the Apple Watch receives with each iteration, battery life is something everyone wants more of. The company touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 lasts for 24 hours on a full charge. Apple measures this using a combination of 300 time checks, 15 minutes of app use, six hours of sleep tracking, 90 notifications and a 60-minute workout alongside music playback. Real-world results will naturally vary depending on how much you use your Apple Watch every day.

If your Apple Watch's battery health has depleted significantly, bringing it in for a battery replacement could help restore its original endurance. You can check battery health status on your watch by navigating to Settings > Battery > Battery Health. Power users might want to look at the Apple Watch Ultra 4 as their next buy since it's better equipped to handle constant, demanding usage with its larger battery.

That said, there are a handful of software tricks you can use to squeeze more battery life out of your existing Apple Watch, especially if it's not yet due for a battery replacement. Some of these are simple toggles to enable, while others involve making small adjustments to how you use your watch throughout the day.

The easiest way to extend your Apple Watch's battery life when it's running low is to turn on Low Power Mode. You can access this feature by pressing the side button, tapping the battery percentage and selecting Low Power Mode.

An information card will display the first time you use this feature — scroll down and tap on Turn On. Alternatively, you can choose to keep Low Power Mode on for one, two or three days if you know you'll be away from a charger for a while. You can also access this battery saver feature by heading to Settings > Battery.

A few changes are immediately noticeable when you turn Low Power Mode on. The Always On display is disabled, as are the Wrist Flick and Double Tap gestures. Your watch will still light up its display automatically when you raise your wrist. Background heart rate and blood oxygen measurements are also paused; you can use their respective apps to get manual readings at any time, but low, high or irregular heart rate notifications are disabled. Losing basic health tracking features can be a dealbreaker to many.

Apple indicates that Siri requests can take longer on the Apple Watch when it's in Low Power Mode, too. Live Activities and the complications on your watch face will enhancement less frequently and scrolling may stutter a bit. Your Apple Watch will continue to receive notifications and calls, but only if its paired iPhone is nearby. When you launch an app that requires internet access, Low Power Mode temporarily turns on Wi-Fi or cellular data.

Sources indicate that the Apple Watch works best when it's near its paired iPhone, but it can also connect to the internet on its own when needed. Any Apple Watch can connect to Wi-Fi networks, while cellular models offer even greater freedom by utilizing mobile data.

Sources indicate that however, Apple recommends keeping the two devices nearby when you need to maximize battery life on your watch. This is because the Apple Watch piggybacks on its paired iPhone's internet connection over Bluetooth. When your devices are connected, you'll spot a tiny green phone icon in Control Center on your Apple Watch.

In a recent development, cellular connectivity is convenient, but if you're somewhere that has Wi-Fi available, using that instead can conserve battery life. When you're not actively using your watch and don't mind it being disconnected for a while, you can stretch its endurance even further by enabling Airplane Mode. Find all these toggles in Control Center or access them through the Settings app.

Even without access to an internet connection, your Apple Watch can track workouts, play music or podcasts that have been downloaded, make purchases using Apple Pay and track your sleep. A good chunk of the built-in apps, like Alarms, Timers, Medications and Voice Memos, also work just fine.

Recent findings suggest that the Apple Watch is much more than just a fitness tracker. It can come in handy when your iPhone isn't nearby and you receive a call or message. Newer models come with improved speakers capable of playing music directly. And when you install an app on your iPhone, your Apple Watch will automatically install its companion version (if available).

In a recent development, this is all great for convenience, but means your watch might end up with a bunch of apps you don't really need on your wrist. Those apps might also increase battery consumption by refreshing in the background and sending you notifications. Using the built-in speakers consumes more battery than connecting headphones does.

Start by uninstalling unneeded apps from your watch directly, which doesn't remove them from your iPhone. If you use an app on your Apple Watch occasionally but don't need it constantly fetching new information, navigate to Settings > General > Background App Refresh and turn its toggle off. It's also an option to disable Background App Refresh entirely, but this will affect all apps on your watch.

In a recent development, you can also disable certain app notifications if you don't want your watch constantly buzzing on your wrist. By default, app notifications you've disabled on your iPhone will also be disabled on your Apple Watch, but you can customize which apps send notifications to your watch independently through the Watch app on your iPhone.

Navigate to Notifications, scroll down to the Mirror iPhone Alerts From section and disable the toggles for any apps you don't want sending notifications to your Apple Watch. Fewer notifications mean fewer vibrations, fewer screen wake-ups and thus potentially less battery drain throughout the day.

In a recent development, for a more granular approach, you're able to turn off Always On display without giving up the other features Low Power Mode shuts off. On your Apple Watch, navigate to Settings > Display & Brightness > Always On and turn the toggle off.

In a recent development, alternatively, this menu has options to customize what information indicates on the Always On display, such as Live Activities or complication data. Macworld tested how substantial of a difference turning this feature off makes, and reported that disabling Always On display extended battery life on the Apple Watch by an impressive 10 to 12 hours.

It has been revealed that to minimize screen-on time, always cover your watch with your palm when you're done using it. You might also want to turn off the Wake on Wrist Raise toggle (in the same menu) to prevent your watch from lighting up accidentally. Since Low Power Mode disables other gestures, it's fair to assume that shutting off features like Double Tap and Wrist Flick could help conserve a little more battery. You can find these toggles by navigating to Settings > Gestures.

If you don't like the barebones feel of the Apple Watch when using Low Power Mode, you can configure it to only kick in during specific workouts. This is a great option if you regularly track longer exercise sessions and are willing to sacrifice some workout tracking features in exchange for longer battery life. In watchOS 27, the Workout app introduced two fresh options that turn Low Power Mode on during workouts.

Recent findings suggest that open the Workout app, select an activity type and tap the Goals and Targets button in the top-right corner. Scroll down and tap on Extended, then select Extended Workout to start tracking your activity. Some workouts have a second Max Extended Workout option as well that reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate measurements. It will also disable alerts, splits and certain metrics like current pace during the workout. Once you finish the exercise, Low Power Mode will automatically turn off.

In a recent development, if you want the battery saver feature to kick in automatically every time you start a workout, navigate to Settings > Workout and turn the Low Power Mode toggle on. This eliminates the need for you to manually select the Extended Workout option each time — it's one of those underrated Apple Watch features that are easy to miss.

Tech Report: Here's when a Raspberry Pi 5 could be considered overkill

  • Recent findings suggest that the ongoing memory shortage has led to price increases across the tech industry, even affecting historically affordable computers like the Raspberry Pi.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Powerful? Yes. Necessary? Maybe not.

Recent findings suggest that the ongoing memory shortage has led to price increases across the tech industry, even affecting historically affordable computers like the Raspberry Pi. In early November 2026, Raspberry Pi CEO Eben Upton announced that the latest Raspberry Pi 5's 16GB variant was getting an $80 price hike. At $385 for the 16GB Pi 5, it's safe to say that the platform is no longer as affordable as it once was. The Pi 5's 2GB, 4GB and 8GB models saw price increases earlier in 2026 too.

It has been revealed that but if you're looking to buy a Raspberry Pi today, you don't have to limit yourself to the newest Pi 5 board. Depending on your intended use case, you could save significant money by buying an older model. The Pi 4, in particular, is still a capable platform with plenty of power for both light desktop use and the typical projects you would run on a Pi. And you're not just saving on the board itself — the Pi 4 has more modest power and cooling requirements than the latest model.

The Raspberry Pi 5 is more than twice as powerful as the previous-generation Pi 4, but you'll only notice that difference in the real world if you use it as your sole computer. The Raspberry Pi 4's slower CPU means it's not as well-suited for web browsing or heavy workloads. But if you're planning to use the board as a springboard for hobbies like self-hosting, home automation or robotics, you're unlikely to find the Pi 4's performance lacking.

Unfortunately, the higher-end Raspberry Pi 4 models have also seen substantial price increases over the past year or so. Still, they remain slightly cheaper than the Pi 5 and more widely available. The Pi 4's official starting price is just $35 for the 1GB model, the same as the original Raspberry Pi that was released in 2012.

The Pi 4's less performant CPU also saves you money on power and cooling. It only needs a 15W USB adapter, which is far more common than the 27W USB-C PD adapter that the Pi 5 required. Additionally, the older Pi 4 runs cooler, and you don't need to add a cooling fan to the bill of materials for most projects. However, the Raspberry Pi 5 tends to exceed 176 degrees Fahrenheit (80 degrees Celsius) after a minute of heavy load. Without a cooling fan, the board then throttles the CPU to bring temperatures under control.

According to recent reports, when you factor in the cost of a more capable power adapter and cooling hardware, the Pi 5 ends up costing more than the $45 starting price would have you believe. The Pi 4's CPU also benefits from cooling hardware, but it doesn't get hot as rapidly and you can get away with a cheap, passive aluminum heatsink.

If you're willing to stomach the extra initial cost of a Raspberry Pi 5 and hunt for available stock, it's definitely the more future-proof option. The Pi 5's 1GB and 2GB RAM variants, in particular, are only slightly more expensive than the Pi 4, but whether those work for you depends on how much RAM you need from your Pi.

In a recent development, that remarked, the advantage to buying an older Raspberry Pi is availability. Many official retailers simply cannot keep the affordable Pi 5 models in stock, while you can easily buy a Pi 4 or 3B+ without waiting for a restock. The $35 Pi 4 is also available at Micro Center locations in the US, while you'd have to order the base model Pi 5 online and pay for shipping.

The used market is also flooded with older Pi 4 boards as people upgrade to either the latest model or a more powerful computer altogether. In my city, I see dozens of listings for Raspberry Pi 4 and 3B+ boards on Facebook Marketplace, all selling well below the current retail price. These deals often include power supplies, cases and other necessary accessories too.

According to recent reports, raspberry Pi boards are safe to buy second-hand as they're surprisingly durable. They don't have any moving parts and most people use them for relatively lightweight loads. Even if you use a Raspberry Pi as a media server, for instance, the board remains idle most of the time. With minimal power draw and heat generation, a Pi can easily last several years if not a decade. So buying a used Raspberry Pi isn't as much of a gamble as a pre-owned desktop.

Raspberry Pi's CEO has called the recent price increases a "difficult, but temporary" phase and committed to lowering prices when memory costs fall. However, memory manufacturers have warned of supply shortages extending into 2028 and beyond. Put simply, the latest Raspberry Pi may come down in cost anytime soon.

How long is a upcoming Fitbit actually supposed to last?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Longevity is a major factor to consider with any fitness wearable.
  • Sources indicate that there's more to longevity than durability, though.
  • Industry observers note that how long can you expect a latest product like the Fitbit Edge or Fitbit Air to last?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Longevity is a major factor to consider with any fitness wearable. It's meant to be used 24/7, and its subject to conditions that would wreck many other products, from accidental knocks and scrapes to heavy deadlift sessions. As gadgets go, there are few things worse than discovering you're out a few hundred dollars because your tracker wasn't sufficiently sweatproof.

Sources indicate that there's more to longevity than durability, though. There's also battery health, not to mention software support, since a tracker is useless if you can't sync and browse its data. At some point, end of support is virtually guaranteed — it's just a question of whether that will be before or after you're ready to move on.

Industry observers note that how long can you expect a latest product like the Fitbit Edge or Fitbit Air to last? While we obviously can't say for certain, info from Google, third parties and my own personal experience with wearables may be helpful.

In a recent development, let's return to durability for a moment. Most impacts are only going to do cosmetic damage, as long as you don't destroy the screen or button(s), so the greater concern is water resistance. A product like the Edge has an IP68 rating, meaning it can be submerged and keep running, but that's only for as long as its liquid protection seals hold up.

Over time, the seals on any device are bound to degrade, especially with repeated exposure to moisture. It's just a question of how promptly. While a person who only wears their Fitbit for walking might never run into trouble, someone who swims daily might encounter a sudden breakdown a few years down the road. Sweat killed three generations of my Beats earbuds, despite their supposed IPX4 sweat and water resistance.

As for battery health, all lithium ion batteries have a finite number of 0 to 100 percent charge cycles. In wearables, this is typically about 300, so charging a device roughly once per week could in theory get you over five years of runtime. That's not the whole picture, however. Apart from variable cycle counts, your device's health can be prolonged if you rarely let your battery go dead, but its lifespan can also be harmed by the glitch of practical capacity.

According to recent reports, before you hit that 300 mark, various chemical factors will probably reduce capacity to the point you no longer consider a Fitbit usable. Most people don't want to charge a wearable multiple times per day. Also, while the Edge has a replaceable battery, it's the exception to the rule. There's no choice but to dispose of most Fitbits once they cross this threshold.

It has been revealed that google explains that it offers security updates for at least two years after a Fitbit product is no longer on sale. If you buy one of the company's current models, updates are going to last through 2028 and probably beyond, depending on when Google refreshes its hardware. The Inspire 3, Versa 4 and Sense 2 will presumably be first on the chopping block, since they introduced in 2022.

It has been revealed that note that security updates aren't the same thing as active feature support. Companies like Google tend to prioritize the newest hardware, both to encourage you to spend money, and because older products can only keep up with feature changes for so long. For example, Google Health Guardian features like irregular rhythm notifications only work with a narrow range of Fitbits, despite some unsupported models having heart rate sensors too. Meanwhile, the original Fitbit app has been replaced by Google Health. There's no telling how long legacy devices will remain compatible as the new app evolves.

You may eventually find features so basic or broken that you end up buying a latest device regardless of damage, battery health or security vulnerabilities. Realistically, I wouldn't count on owning a new Fitbit for any more than five years, but I hope I'm proven wrong.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This tool allows you to search for exactly the type of content you want to see.

In a recent development, youTube is a core hub of entertainment for millions of people. More than 20 million videos hit the platform every day, according to data from YouTube. That's a lot of content to sort through when you're trying to find something to watch. If you're a regular watcher of YouTube, your homepage is probably already leaning into your interests, be they comedy specials, home improvement tutorials or music videos from the '90s. But if you're looking to exert some more control and specificity over what the algorithm suggests to you, YouTube has a way to do it by offloading your playlist curation to AI.

Sources indicate that as of October 2026, the platform introduced custom feeds. In short, custom feeds let you use natural language to set up feeds around the kind of content you want to see more of and keep it in a spot that's easy to access. Here's how to set up those feeds if you want to fine-tune your homepage.

If you want to tailor what you're seeing on YouTube more to your tastes, you can start by building a custom feed using prompts. At the top of your homepage, tap the + sign (you may also see the words "Custom feed"). From there, you can type into the box whatever you are interested in seeing. For example, YouTube gives examples like "I want retro tech nostalgia: 80s commercials, vintage PCs, CRT glow." Another example indicates that you don't even have to get that specific. You could ask for a feed along the lines of, "I want to explore something completely different beyond my usual feed.".

Once you create a feed, you'll find it at the top of the screen so you can access it when you want. YouTube noted that you can always use the prompt box at the top of a feed if you want to tweak what you're seeing.

According to recent reports, if you like the idea of custom feeds, you can save up to three without a YouTube Premium account. If you do happen to have a YouTube Premium account, you can save up to eight. Regardless of your subscription, as long as you are signed into your account, the custom feeds you created will sync across mobile and desktop. It's also crucial to remember that custom feeds will expire if you don't use them for 30 days. If this happens, though, you can always create a newly introduced prompt. YouTube also pointed out that the feeds are subject to the platform's community guidelines.

According to recent reports, so far, custom feeds are only available in English in the United States. You also need to have search history enabled to use the feature.

The rollout of custom feeds wasn't the only change YouTube brought to the homepage. Specifically on the mobile app, you might have noticed a row of feeds across the top of the page with categories like Live or Music. Some of these feeds might depend on your subscription. For example, you won't see the Movies & TV feed if you don't have any Primetime Channel subscriptions. Additionally, YouTube mentioned that the Subs feed, as in your subscriptions, moved to the top bar. If you want to exit your feeds, you can always tap on the Home tab on the left and go back to what you'd normally see on your homepage.

In its blogpost, YouTube stated these changes are part of a series of updates to shape "a more seamless Home experience." So, if you're looking to create some feeds based on more specific interests that you can easily get to from the homepage, YouTube's custom feeds feature might be worth a prompt.

The advantages of using a USB-C docking station

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plus, there are differences between a USB-C hub and a docking station.
  • Sources indicate that laptops have been getting thinner and lighter from year to year, and they have become so powerful that many people choose a laptop as their main computer.
  • A USB-C docking station is a box that connects to your laptop through a single USB-C cable and gives it a full set of ports.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus, there are differences between a USB-C hub and a docking station.

Sources indicate that laptops have been getting thinner and lighter from year to year, and they have become so powerful that many people choose a laptop as their main computer. But a thin body means fewer ports, and a desktop setup with a screen, mouse, webcam and keyboard requires a lot of them. If you have a laptop and still want the full desktop experience, a USB-C docking station can be the solution you're looking for.

A USB-C docking station is a box that connects to your laptop through a single USB-C cable and gives it a full set of ports. USB-C docking stations reduce cord clutter, add more ports to your setup and can keep your laptop's own ports from wearing down.

The biggest advantage of a dock is simplicity. One single cable connects the laptop to its peripherals. That means you can come home and plug in all your devices with one plug; you can also grab your laptop on your way out just as quickly. Monitors, a keyboard, a webcam and a charger no longer need to be reconnected every time the laptop comes and goes, and your desk stays tidier because the cables run to the dock instead of the laptop.

It has been revealed that A dock can also add ports your laptop doesn't have. Depending on the model, you can get HDMI or DisplayPort outputs for external monitors, more USB ports, an SD card reader and an Ethernet port for a stable wired internet connection. A thin laptop that comes with three or four ports can end up with a dozen.

Industry observers note that the third advantage is less wear on your laptop. Plugging and unplugging several cables over and over puts strain on the ports, and a dock takes that job over. Instead of plugging several cables into the laptop every day, you plug in just one.

Recent findings suggest that if you only need a few basic connections, a USB-C hub is the cheaper option. Hubs have roughly four to 10 ports and cost anywhere between $30 and $150. Docking stations generally have more ports, come with their own DC power adapter, and cost more, with some higher-end models costing more than $400. A dock can give you a full desktop setup with multiple monitors, plus more ports of every kind, and the higher-end Thunderbolt 4 and USB4 models can run multiple displays, Ethernet, audio and laptop charging through that one cable. If that sounds like what you need, here are the best docking stations for laptops.

In a recent development, before buying, it's worth checking a few things, because not every dock works with every laptop. A USB-C port only outputs video if it supports DisplayPort Alt Mode or is a Thunderbolt or USB4 port, and the dock needs to support Power Delivery pass-through at your laptop's required wattage. If you initiative to work with the lid closed, keep the power plugged in, since the laptop draws more power with an external monitor attached.

Get those details right and a dock quietly does its job, providing a laptop that goes back to being portable by unplugging just one cable.

You don't need a foldable phone to use split screen on Android

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that despite all odds, folding smartphones have stuck around.
  • Split screen multitasking has been around since Android 7.0 Nougat, which was released a decade ago in 2016.
  • This can be accessed by swiping up from the very bottom and holding on the screen if you're using gesture navigation, or by tapping the Recents button if you use the three-button navigation system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slab-style phones can do this trick too.

Sources indicate that despite all odds, folding smartphones have stuck around. They've mostly found their place in two  categories: flip phones that fold a regular-sized smartphone in half for portability and book-style phones that unfold to reveal a larger canvas. For years, foldables like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 have been marketed as productivity machines, allowing you to get more things done on a device you carry around in your pocket. Split screen multitasking is often highlighted as one of their biggest selling points, but you don't need to set aside close to $2,000 just to use two apps at the same time.

Split screen multitasking has been around since Android 7.0 Nougat, which was released a decade ago in 2016. In fact, the feature was first discovered in Android 6.0 Marshmallow, though it required root access. All modern Android smartphones should come with this multitasking feature out of the box, but the exact steps to activate it might differ depending on your phone's manufacturer and Android version. Most phones, including ones from Google, Samsung and Motorola, let you enable split screen multitasking through the recent apps switcher.

This can be accessed by swiping up from the very bottom and holding on the screen if you're using gesture navigation, or by tapping the Recents button if you use the three-button navigation system. All of your opened apps will be listed here. Tap on an app's icon and select Split Screen from the options that show up. You can now select a second app that you want open alongside the first one. You can further adjust how much space each app occupies by dragging the divider in the middle. Dragging it all the way up or down will exit the split screen mode.

According to recent reports, most traditional slab-style Android phones only let you use a maximum of two apps at once in split screen view — not that you'd realistically want to cram a third one onto such a small display anyway. This is where larger foldables let you take multitasking a step further by accommodating three or more apps at the same time. That remarked, split screen view isn't the only multitasking feature that Android offers.

In a recent development, modern Android phones also let you use apps in floating windows, which allows for a slightly different kind of multitasking. Instead of splitting your screen in two halves, a floating window appears on top of whatever app you're currently using. This lets you view and interact with two apps simultaneously without splitting the screen. You can move the floating window around or resize it by grabbing its edges or corners.

Different manufacturers handle this feature differently. Pixel phones running Android 17, for instance, offer the Bubbles feature, which lets you use floating apps that collapse into Facebook Messenger-style chat heads when minimized, allowing you to open them quickly without leaving your current app. Samsung calls this feature Pop-up view while some manufacturers like OnePlus and Oppo simply label it Floating Windows.

It has been revealed that colorOS 17 handles it particularly well, even allowing you to change the aspect ratio of certain floating windows. My OnePlus 15 can accommodate two apps in split screen view and a third one running in a floating window on top, though I'm yet to find a use case that warrants this level of multitasking madness on a slab-style phone.

It has been revealed that though the feature has been around for a hot minute, you may find the split view mode not working in some cases. App compatibility has improved a lot over the years, but there are still a few apps that might not work in multiwindow setups. When this is the case, you'll either find the Split View option greyed out or simply missing. It's still worth heading to the Play Store and updating all of your apps to see if an app's newer version might introduce support for split screen multitasking.

According to recent reports, if not, this is Android we're talking about, so of course there's a workaround. Hidden away in the Developer Options menu is the Force activities to be resizable toggle. Turning this on might let you force split screen mode for apps that don't officially support it. This might not always work, though. For instance, it seemed to do the trick for all unsupported apps on my older Android phone, but I didn't have the same luck on my current device. There's also no guarantee that unsupported apps will play nicely in split screen view.

Sources indicate that the Developer Options menu is hidden by default. To enable it, navigate to Settings > About, look for the Build Number entry and tap on it seven times. Enter your PIN or password when prompted. Once enabled, you can find the hidden menu under Settings > System on most phones. While simply having Developer Options enabled isn't inherently dangerous, it does hold many advanced settings that might affect your phone's performance and stability, so it's best to leave anything you're not familiar with unchanged.

Industry News: What the tiny key icon means on your Android device

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Android status bar is designed to give users important information at a glance, but all those icons can blur together.
  • More specifically, that icon is a visual indicator that you're connected via a VPN that encrypts your web traffic from third parties.
  • In a recent development, if you use a VPN but don't want the key icon taking up space in your status bar, you're out of luck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Android status bar is designed to give users important information at a glance, but all those icons can blur together. One of the most unusual symbols looks like a leftward-facing key with two teeth opposite its circular handle. That icon tells you that your internet connection is encrypted, but there's nothing to worry about.

More specifically, that icon is a visual indicator that you're connected via a VPN that encrypts your web traffic from third parties. Many people consider a VPN crucial for their online security, and modern Android versions support VPNs at the OS level. The key icon, then, lets users know they're safe behind their VPN, while its absence alerts them that their encryption has been broken, giving them a chance to address it.

In a recent development, if you use a VPN but don't want the key icon taking up space in your status bar, you're out of luck. Because it's a security and privacy feature, most Android devices don't have a built-in option to remove the icon. Only Samsung Galaxy owners can do so, and even then, they'll need to download the Good Lock customization suite from the Galaxy Store and go into the QuickStar module to toggle the key indicator and other icons.

The key icon appears only when a VPN is active, so the only way to get rid of it is to disable the VPN. If you're running a third-party VPN, open the app and turn it off from there. Some VPN apps even keep a notification active with a button to turn them off, making it an even quicker process. On a Pixel or other close-to-stock Android device, you can also swipe into Quick Settings and tap the number next to the profile icon at the bottom of the screen to show active background apps, then tap Stop next to your VPN.

If you don't know which VPN you're running, open your phone's Settings app and go to Network & internet > VPN, then tap on it from the list there. On Samsung Galaxy phones, go to Settings > Connections > More connection settings > VPN to find a functionally identical screen. If you are connected to a VPN, it will be shown on a list with text underneath reading "Connected." Tap the running VPN and choose Disconnect. If you are not connected to a VPN, tap a VPN, and you will be taken to its app, where you can connect.

Industry observers note that tapping the settings gear icon next to any VPN will allow you to configure it further. If you want to configure a VPN manually, you can tap the plus icon in the top right, but this is generally recommended for advanced owners. For more, see our guide on how to use a VPN. All other aspects of your VPN can be managed within its proprietary app. Since every VPN has a different interface in its app, consult your provider's documentation if you're not sure how to use a feature or setting.

Sources indicate that if you don't use a VPN, you may wonder whether it's worth installing one on your Android phone. How useful one will be depends largely on how privacy-minded you are, your streaming habits and whether you already have a VPN or need to get a subscription first.

Industry observers note that another classic use case is making it appear as though you are somewhere you're not, usually to access geofenced content. For instance, Netflix may offer demonstrates in other countries that it doesn't in your own due to licensing deals, and a VPN will let you set your location to those regions to access that content.

While VPNs offer benefits, they can cause concerns when browsing the web. Some websites will treat your device as inherently suspicious when it connects from a VPN IP address, and you may encounter more anti-automation measures such as CAPTCHAs. Some websites may even be totally unresponsive until you disconnect your VPN. Despite that, if you already pay for a service that includes a VPN, it may be worth enabling it to get a taste of what using a VPN is like on your phone. Otherwise, have a gander at our list of the best VPNs in 2026.

These iOS settings will help you control your mobile data use

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avoid data overage charges or speed thorttling with these iOS settings.
  • Cellular connectivity is now fast and reliable enough to rival home broadband, especially with 5G.
  • The iPhone offers a handful of built-in settings that can help you monitor and manage mobile data use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Avoid data overage charges or speed thorttling with these iOS settings.

Cellular connectivity is now fast and reliable enough to rival home broadband, especially with 5G. But telcos typically aren't as generous about data allowances. If you don't watch your data use, you may end up with hefty bills — if your telco charges for excess data — or painfully slow speeds once you exceed your monthly allowance. You consume cellular data not just when you're downloading a file or watching a video, either: background app refresh, app updates and cloud syncing can also eat into your data allowance bit by bit.

The iPhone offers a handful of built-in settings that can help you monitor and manage mobile data use. Firstly, you can view a list of apps and how much data they use by heading to Settings > Cellular, scrolling down to the Cellular Data section and tapping on Show All. This will list mobile data use for individual apps you have installed. You can sort these apps by name or usage to quickly identify which ones consume the most data.

Tap the toggle next to any app to prevent it from using cellular data. The app will stop updating its content in the background when you're not connected to Wi-Fi and might also stop sending you notifications. The next time you launch the app, it will alert you that mobile data has been turned off for the app and give you the option to re-enable it.

Industry observers note that if you rely mainly on Wi-Fi, turning off mobile data can prevent data usage and reduce battery drain. Navigate to Settings > Cellular to toggle Cellular Data on or off. iOS also lets you limit data consumption, so you can keep cellular data on without exhausting your monthly allowance as quickly. In Cellular settings, navigate to Cellular Data Options > Data Mode and select Low Data Mode. This setting might be set to Standard by default, which allows automatic updates and background tasks even when you're not on Wi-Fi. Low Data Mode restricts this, reducing your mobile data use.

According to recent reports, being connected to Wi-Fi doesn't guarantee that your iPhone won't consume mobile data. Head to Settings > Wi-Fi, scroll down and turn the Connectivity Assist toggle off. Before iOS 27, this feature was called Wi-Fi Assist and could be found under Settings > Cellular. The feature keeps your iPhone constantly connected to the internet, but it uses mobile data to do so. When a Wi-Fi connection becomes too weak or busy, Connectivity Assist switches to cellular data to keep you connected to the internet. If you don't mind potential disruptions, turning this feature off may reduce unexpected mobile data use.

It has been revealed that beyond the Settings app, there are other ways you can restrict mobile data use on your iPhone. For starters, changing automatic update behavior can help avoid unexpected cellular activity. Navigate to Settings > Apps > App Store and, under the Mobile Data section, turn the Automatic Downloads toggle off. Open the Settings app, tap on your name at the top, navigate to iCloud > iCloud Backup and make sure the Back Up Over Mobile Data toggle is unchecked.

If you stream music regularly, check the audio quality in your app of choice. Apple Music people can find this option by navigating to Settings > Apps > Music > Audio Quality > Data Streaming. Lossless audio may provide a superior listening experience, but it is an absolute data hog. Other apps, like Tidal, Spotify and YouTube Music, also let you reduce audio quality when using mobile data. Lowering video quality to 720p on YouTube can also help manage data consumption. You can also reduce how much data your navigation apps use by downloading maps for offline use; both Apple Maps and Google Maps let you do so.

Lastly, you can look for toggles and features in third-party apps designed to reduce cellular usage. For instance, you can stop WhatsApp from automatically downloading media from newly introduced chats by tapping your profile picture, navigating to Storage and data and setting the Media auto-download option for photos, videos and documents to Wi-Fi. Instagram fans can find a Use less mobile data toggle by opening the app's settings page and navigating to Media quality.

How Secure Is Your Password? Here's How To Test It

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what a strong password looks like and how to check whether yours would hold up against hackers, plus a few habits that keep accounts safer.
  • Recent findings suggest that remember the old days when you'd try to use "1234" or "password" as your password?
  • But even if you think you have created a password that Robert Langdon from The Da Vinci Code himself couldn't crack, how do you truly know how secure it is?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what a strong password looks like and how to check whether yours would hold up against hackers, plus a few habits that keep accounts safer.

Recent findings suggest that remember the old days when you'd try to use "1234" or "password" as your password? There really was never a time when passwords like those were secure. Thankfully, nowadays, most services don't even permit you to use passwords that aren't secure enough. They require a combination of letters, numbers and symbols along with different letter cases before accepting your chosen password. It makes passwords tougher to remember on the one hand, but it's essential in this day and age to ensure that your password can't be easily cracked by nefarious individuals or even AI systems.

But even if you think you have created a password that Robert Langdon from The Da Vinci Code himself couldn't crack, how do you truly know how secure it is? Usually, if it includes all the elements noted above, especially if the letters do not connect to spell an actual word, you're in a good spot.

Sources indicate that to know for sure, you can run it through a free password strength checker, such as the one at Security.org. However, remember that creating a secure password is just one of the steps you can take to be safer online.

It's important to understand what makes a good password in the first place. It should be at least 12 characters, and in fact, many sites do not let you submit a password that is less than that anyway. Along with the aforementioned upper and lower case letters, numbers and symbols, keep in mind that the letters should not spell a discernible, and certainly not an identifiable word like your surname. They should also not be consecutive in the alphabet, like "LMNOP," or in a row on a keyboard, like "QWERTY." The same goes for numbers, which should be random instead of something like your birthday or street address. The letters and numbers should not be repeated as well, like "BBB" or "555.".

Once you create a password you think is secure, enter it into the Security.org checker, which evaluates it and provides feedback. As you type, the site shows how long it would take a computer to crack the password. The more characters you add, the longer this duration becomes. I went from a password with letters and numbers that would take four years to figure out to one with symbols that bumps it to 2 million years before someone could crack it. It's safe to say both are secure, but the latter is more secure. When I tried using a simple word with consecutive numbers, it advised that the password could be cracked in three days.

When creating an account, you might see an option to "create a strong password" automatically after which you can save it to password memory, like Apple MacBook's Passwords app or a third-party password manager like 1Password. It's a good idea to use these even over signing in with an existing Google, Apple or other account. There are convenience benefits to doing that, but for extra security, create a latest login.

Sources indicate that there are pros and cons of using a password manager over an authenticator app, but there's no reason you can't use both. If the site offers passkeys versus passwords, these are worth using. They can be more secure, relying on a private key accessed through biometrics (your fingerprint or face) or a PIN.

Along with having a secure password, it is also notable to make every password unique. If you use the same password for everything, no matter how secure, what happens if someone gains access to it from one account? This could happen through a breach or even human error, and it would unlock all your accounts and services. Keeping passwords secure and unique to every service and changing them every 60 to 90 days or immediately if a breach has been reported will keep you as safe as possible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • More efficient solar panels aren't always the better buy.
  • At first glance, all the solar panels in your neighborhood may look much the same, but what they're made of can decide how much power they generate.
  • But just because a certain panel technology is more efficient doesn't instantly make it the best choice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More efficient solar panels aren't always the better buy. Your roof, budget and plans for backup power have a say too.

At first glance, all the solar panels in your neighborhood may look much the same, but what they're made of can decide how much power they generate. Monocrystalline panels tend to generate more power per square foot compared to older polycrystalline models. And when skylights, chimneys and vents already take up some of the sunniest spots, picking the right solar panel can matter.

But just because a certain panel technology is more efficient doesn't instantly make it the best choice. External factors like your electricity consumption, how much shade the panels get and what your utility pays for surplus energy can change the math considerably, so it can pay to size your system using the 20 percent rule for solar panels. That means building in enough capacity to produce around 20 percent more energy than your household normally uses as a buffer for dimmer days. At the same time, inverters, mounting hardware and labor for installing the equipment need to be accounted for too (no matter how compelling the brochure seems).

There's also the burning question of what you'll be powering up with those solar panels. Someone hoping to shave off some bucks on their monthly bill needs a different setup from one who needs their Wi-Fi and kitchen appliances to survive the next power outage.

According to recent reports, between the monocrystalline cells (built from a single crystal of silicon) and polycrystalline cells, the former do pack a higher power density. These polycrystalline panels could be cheaper where they're still available, but they also take up more space to produce comparable power. Thin-film panels, on the other hand, are built from thin layers of photovoltaic material, and while some are flexible and light enough for unconventional mounting, they're hardly ever the first choice for a traditional pitched roof.

Modern monocrystalline panels come with cell technologies like TOPCon, HJT and PERC, just to name a few. While most of these aren't based on entirely new materials, each has its own merits for boosting overall cell performance. Let's take Qcells' n-type Q.TRON BLK M-G2+, for instance, which can deliver 440W at 22.5 percent module efficiency, while Tesla's 420W residential module is at least 20.5 percent efficient. Of course, it wouldn't be a fair comparison without factoring in the size of the panels, but neither vendor's specifications alone can give you a breakdown of how much power the panels will pump out for your specific roof.

According to recent reports, and it isn't entirely dependent on sunlight either, since solar panels tend to become less efficient as they get warmer. Plus, factors like shading and orientation of the panels can also make a sizable dent in the annual output. Sure, bifacial panels do exist for capturing reflected light from the back end, but this benefit is mostly dependent on how they are mounted, along with the environment.

Sources indicate that to give you some context, the Solar Energy Industries Association reported that the price of an average US residential installation was $3.36 per watt in the second quarter of 2026. For perspective, one of our editors spent just over $24,000 on a 5.1kW installation, including inspections and permits. The federal residential clean energy tax credit ended for setups completed after December 31, 2025, but some state and local incentives may still apply.

Sources indicate that you're spending a small fortune on solar panels, but the good part is that they usually lose output over time rather than suddenly dying on you after a few years. That's why taking a long and hard look at performance warranties could sometimes be just as key as looking at the upfront cost.

Industry observers note that if the cost of a permanent rooftop array seems too much and backup power is your main goal, you can get a portable power station instead. Brands like Anker SOLIX, Jackery, BLUETTI and EcoFlow sell units that can charge up from a single panel or several compatible solar panels to keep a limited number of appliances powered on during a power outage.

Your phone camera is useful for more than just food pics.

In a recent development, smartphones are capable of many impressive and useful feats, from capturing detailed images of objects as far away as the moon to serving as a key part of our home security systems. But smartphones are also useful for much more mundane tasks, such as helping us figure out whether our TV remote's batteries are dead.

It has been revealed that when you press a button on your remote control, it sends that command to your TV using infrared light. While many modern televisions ship with Bluetooth remotes that support features like voice control, they may still rely on an infrared emitter for basic functions like turning the TV on or off. The emitter is located at the front of the remote. It's a tiny LED on the front of the remote that's usually easy to spot, although some modern remotes hide it behind a dark plastic window.

Industry observers note that to test your battery, launch your phone's Camera app, point it at the front of your remote and press and hold a button while looking at your phone's screen. The remote's power button is probably best, since many Bluetooth remotes still use infrared for that command. If you see a flashing light, usually slightly purple, on the front of your remote, it means the batteries still have enough power.

The camera trick also helps you check whether your remote control uses infrared or Bluetooth for other buttons. If you press, say, the volume control and don't see a flashing light, then that command uses Bluetooth. Now, while this is a pretty cool trick, it can't diagnose every remote control problem. For example, a damaged button might not register your presses at all, so you might not see the infrared emitter flash even if your remote's batteries are working perfectly fine.

It has been revealed that for example, the Google Home app works with smart TVs powered by Google TV and Android TV. You can navigate the user interface using D-pad controls, adjust the volume or search for movie titles faster using your phone's keyboard. If the virtual remote won't turn your TV on, you may need to configure your TV's network standby settings. Some models call this feature Wake-on-LAN. Once enabled, you'll never need to worry about dead batteries in your remote control again.

Anthropic logo, Guilherand-Granges, France, March 2025.

In a recent development, mmathematician at Anthropic says he has used the manufacturer’s Claude AI model to prove the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Levent Alpöge made the claim in a note on his website on Friday, Bloomberg reported.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote.

According to recent reports, the hypothesis, first proposed in 1859, concerns how prime numbers are spread out. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven Millennium Prize Problems, each of which carries a $1m prize. Alpöge says his proof also covers a broader version, the generalised Riemann hypothesis.

According to recent reports, he did not publish a traditional paper. Instead, he released the proof in Lean, a programming language that checks every logical step. The code runs to about 17 million lines, Science reported.

Sources indicate that andrew Sutherland, a senior research scientist at MIT, told Bloomberg he had checked the code on his own computer. He mentioned he had seen at least three other checks by professional mathematicians. Later on Friday, Sutherland put the chance that anything is wrong at roughly zero, Scientific American reported.

In a recent development, however, other mathematicians urged caution. A proof that compiles in Lean still has to state the right problem, and humans have to confirm that it does.

Kevin Buzzard, a professor at Imperial College London, mentioned nobody yet understands what the proof demonstrates, Al Jazeera reported. The proof has not been formally accepted.

Alpöge said Claude did much of the work.

“This time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” he wrote.

Anthropic declined to comment to Bloomberg. The claim came a day after the company’s record stock market debut.

Recent findings suggest that if confirmed, it would be the second Millennium Prize Problem that AI may have helped solve. In September, OpenAI mentioned its models had produced a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem.

Meta did not immediately return a request for comment.

Can a TV be too large? An investigation

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED.
  • Industry observers note that the organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry.
  • Industry observers note that they are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED.

Industry observers note that the organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows.

In short: They look way better.

Industry observers note that they are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the company’s mid-range unit released in 2024.

At first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic.

However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache.

I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their massive new toy is breaking their brain.

“I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor, who said they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.”.

Others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too massive and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?”.

There doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen.

In a recent development, finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. I dialed down the brightness on mine to around 50 percent, although I had doubts as to whether this actually had anything to do with the feelings I was having.

In considering my nausea, one theory that sprang to mind was that it might just be my eyes’ inexperience with viewing such a major screen. The TV was so large that it often felt like my eye had to trace different parts of the screen to take in the whole picture and, if the scene involved significant motion (most movie scenes do, after all), it conjured the sensation of trying to stare too intently at something out the window of a moving car.

It has been revealed that after a few days, however, my eyes finally adjusted. The nausea was gone. All that remained was an immense and beautiful home viewing experience that made every previous viewing experience pale by comparison.

According to recent reports, initial physiological reactions aside, the size of the 65-inch screen (and whether your living space actually has room for it) is still something that needs to be considered carefully by potential buyers. I recently moved into a place with a slightly bigger living room, which has given me the flexibility to install a bigger device. At my old apartment, however, this size of TV would have definitely felt like it was devouring the space.

It has been revealed that another slight frustration is that the C4 does not come with any detailed installation instructions. The screen (which is so wide it’s difficult to move without another person there to help you) comes detached from its base, and the user is just sort of expected to figure out how to effectively move and put together the two pieces. A quick YouTube video is all that is necessary to understand this process, but you have to be careful when moving and assembling the pieces so as not to scratch or damage the screen.

Industry observers note that once the whole thing is set up and assembled, the OLED is a truly beautiful thing to behold. The customization that’s possible, including advanced brightness and color control — and things like “Filmmaker Mode” (which claims to adjust each movie’s color and frame rate settings to those intended by the director) — make the user experience really powerful.

To sum up: The evo C4 is a really spectacular piece of equipment that has a lot to offer the avid home entertainment viewer — although there may be a bit of a learning curve before it makes your cinema dreams come true.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you're someone who spends a decent amount of time in front of a computer, perhaps at work or during long gaming sessions, you may have noticed just how finicky certain parts of your computer can be.
  • Turning on your monitor and noticing some unusual oddities, specifically flickering, may seem like an apocalyptic beginning to your day.
  • If it's something more difficult to solve — something deeper at a hardware level — that can become a bit harder to resolve on your own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your screen might be telling you something.

Recent findings suggest that if you're someone who spends a decent amount of time in front of a computer, perhaps at work or during long gaming sessions, you may have noticed just how finicky certain parts of your computer can be. That's especially true of its peripherals and accessories, with one of the usual suspects being your monitor.

Turning on your monitor and noticing some unusual oddities, specifically flickering, may seem like an apocalyptic beginning to your day. Monitors of decent quality are pretty affordable today, but no one wants to spend money on a new display if they don't have to. Thankfully, your computer monitor is fairly easy to troubleshoot on a basic level in order to determine your ideal path forward.

If it's something more difficult to solve — something deeper at a hardware level — that can become a bit harder to resolve on your own. Taking some simple steps to determine the cause and potential fixes can save you a lot of headaches in the long run.

A monitor starting to flicker could stem from a rather wide variety of different complications. One of the most common reasons for a flickering monitor is a loose or potentially faulty display cable, whether that's a modern HDMI or DisplayPort cable, or even an older VGA one. Reinserting the cables or checking them for damage or fraying can be a quick fix.

If you are suspicious that the cable is defective, you could also try swapping the cable out for a new one. If it's not the cable, it may potentially be a bad port on the monitor or the PC itself, which would necessitate trying a different port on the monitor or computer if they have more than one. If you're uncertain which one may potentially be causing the problem, you could also try hooking the monitor up to a different computer that you know with absolute certainty works. If it works without issue, you know who the culprit is.

In a recent development, barring a connection matter of some kind, a flickering monitor can also be caused by something at a software level. The first things to look into are your graphics drivers. Out-of-date graphics drivers are one of the most common causes of display problems, and a simple enhancement to them may be just what you need. On the other hand, a graphics driver update does have the potential to actually cause display problems, so rolling back to a previous version could also work.

You may also be running into an problem with the monitor's refresh rate. For example, if your monitor runs at 120Hz but your Windows 11 PC's refresh rate is set to something entirely different, it can cause some havoc. In order to fix this, all you need to do is go to Settings, then find System on the left panel, then look for Display. Look for Advanced display, then change the refresh rate to match your monitor.

According to recent reports, if you find that your flickering monitor can't be fixed by any normal means, it may be time to look at the issues a little deeper. A consistent, almost shuttering flicker is a surefire sign that the monitor is about to crash and burn. That's especially true when you're unable to solve the matter at a hardware or software level.

The monitor may also experience blackouts, as in sudden hard cuts to black, before returning to normal operation. Your display is quite keen about letting you know when something has gone haywire, and you can do a lot of diagnosing by just examining how your display is behaving.

According to recent reports, faded, dim colors or vertical lines that are swimming through the screen are also a couple of telltale signs. If you think of your monitor like you would a TV and utilize similar modalities, you'll be able to diagnose it in a similar way. If you've already exhausted all your other options but still find that your display looks unhealthy, then it most likely is.

It has been revealed that at this point, your options really narrow themselves down to two. You can either look for someone to repair the monitor or seek out a replacement. Whether you should replace or repair the monitor ultimately depends on your budget, but the price of latest OLED and 4K screens is starting to tumble. In most cases, it may be better to sell it for parts or donate it and just buy something new.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The debut LP from Sheherazaad blends traditional Indian instruments with Western electronic flourishes and feminist narratives.

The debut LP from Sheherazaad blends traditional Indian instruments with Western electronic flourishes and feminist narratives.

In a recent development, sheherazaad started making ripples in the music world a few years ago with her EP Qasr, which was produced by Grammy Award winner Arooj Aftab. Now she’s back with Khudgarzi, her reverb-drenched folk-noir debut LP that’s primarily sung in Urdu.

Recent findings suggest that the instrumentation on Khudgarzi draws on traditional South Asian music, including Carnatic and Hindustani styles, but also dabbles in Arabic folk traditions, as well as modern Western electronic music. Trip-hop flourishes and Spaghetti Western guitar brush up against tanbur and ghatam. Sheherazaad’s stunning voice sits atop dripping percussion and seasick drones singing about the plight of “The Selfish Woman.”.

According to recent reports, for Sheherazaad, the character of the selfish woman isn’t the villain, it’s a charge leveled at women who didn’t conform to societal norms, “eccentric women whose desire for agency was often met with an awful end.” Even if you can’t understand most of the lyrics, the atmosphere tells the story clearly enough. From the barely simmering anger of “Registaan” to the bleak repetition of “Qatil” and the fantastical yearning of “Zeher,” Khudgarzi is clearly the work of a woman exploring what it means to be a woman, the lasting legacy of colonialism, and the perpetual threats of a patriarchal society.

Industry observers note that khudgarzi is alternately a funeral dirge and a celebration of femininity. Sheherazaad owes a lot of the album’s ability to navigate these various themes and moods to her impressive production work, top-notch mixing by J. Valleau, and the cast of over 30 “genre-chaotic” virtuosic musicians including Ria Modak, Sarathy Korwar, Jay Chakravorty, Shunya, and Qasim Naqvi. The instrumentation never distracts, though. It’s not showy, and all emulsifies around Sheherazaad’s vocals in a shawl that feels equal parts comforting and oppressive.

Khudgarzi is available now on Bandcamp and most major streaming platforms, including YouTube Music, Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer, and Qobuz.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry.

There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance?

A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink.

Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world.

A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services.

Industry observers note that uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available.

Industry observers note that uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.

Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he noted. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.).

That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too.

It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers.

You might have seen the Wall Street Journal scoop that General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify possible candidates to replace CEO Mary Barra. Rumors of her imminent departure have swirled for months, but this time there appears to be real work happening behind the scenes.

I reached out to a few little birds to learn more and here’s what they’re telling me. And, for the record, GM declined to comment.

It has been revealed that GM has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles, according to one source, who noted it’s possible that the board has other executive search firms working on this as well. The board is taking a two-track approach to its search, which is occurring simultaneously.

Recent findings suggest that the first is focused on traditional yet transformative automotive CEOs. One name that has come up from the executive search firm is José Muñoz, who is president and CEO of Hyundai. The board is also interested in someone less traditional. The firm has apparently floated names like Doug Field, who recently became CEO of Mind Robotics, and Larry Culp of GE, according to a source with direct information.

There are internal GM folks who are also in the mix, including Sterling Anderson, co-founder of self-driving trucks manufacturer Aurora who became chief product officer at GM in May 2025, and Paul Jacobson, the company’s executive vice president and chief financial officer.

Redwood Materials is using computer vision and machine learning to identify and sort batteries by chemistry before they’re fed into the tech giant’s rotary calciner — a massive cylindrical industrial furnace used to process 40,000 metric tons of raw feedstock a year.

Tesla mentioned it will spend about $3.3 billion to expand its Berlin gigafactory to produce Cybercabs — yet another signal of the firm’s global autonomy ambitions.

Sources indicate that over the weekend, Tesla invited “select customers” to preorder the tech giant’s autonomous, golden Cybercab “for personal use.” The Cybercab is priced at $29,990, but there is a lot more to ownership. The company will charge owners $299 a month to use the vehicles, delivery will only occur in a handful of cities, and operations will be limited to specific locations.

Sources indicate that uber opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities. Uber already has a service for teenagers. If this program proves successful, it would open Uber up to another market of customers: busy families.

Meanwhile, Uber stated it’s notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal information was stolen in an October data breach.

It has been revealed that zipline continues to scale its autonomous drone delivery business, this time in its partnership with Uber. The companies had previously announced a partnership for drones to deliver for Uber Eats, but it officially launched this week in a Houston suburb. The aim is a significant one: Uber and Zipline say they aim to make 1 million deliveries a day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.

And the best part? It's now available for less than $200.

Recent findings suggest that the TCL NXTPAPER 11 Plus combines a paper-like display with the flexibility of a full Android tablet. It features an 11.5-inch 2.2K 120Hz screen, three display modes, 256GB of storage, and an 8,000mAh battery with 33W fast charging.

✅ Recommended if: You want a paper-like display for reading, prefer a larger screen for books and PDFs, or want an affordable Android tablet that handles streaming, browsing, and everyday tasks.

❌ Skip this deal if: You want the weeks-long battery life of a dedicated Kindle, prefer a smaller e-reader, or need a powerful tablet for demanding games and heavy multitasking.

It has been revealed that TCL has been making NXTPAPER devices for a while now, and the NXTPAPER 11 Plus is one of the more interesting tablets in its lineup. Unlike other NXTPAPER tablets, this tablet lets you switch between three different modes, including Regular Mode, Color Paper Mode, and Ink Paper Mode, simply by pressing the dedicated NXTPAPER Key on the tablet.

You can use the regular mode when watching videos or browsing the web, switch to Color Paper Mode for a more comfortable reading experience, or use Ink Paper Mode for a more traditional black-and-white e-reader feel.

It has been revealed that speaking of display, the NXTPAPER 11 Plus comes with a 11.5-inch display with a 2.2K resolution and a smooth 120Hz refresh rate. That said, the best part of this tablet is probably its design.

According to recent reports, it is only 0.26 inches thin and weighs around 1.08 pounds. That makes it easy to toss into your backpack before a flight or carry around throughout the day without adding much weight. TCL has also given it a metal body, so you're not getting a cheap-feeling plastic tablet despite the affordable price.

In a recent development, battery life shouldn't be much of a concern either. The NXTPAPER 11 Plus packs a sizable 8,000mAh battery, which should be plenty for long reading sessions, watching movies, or getting through a day of regular use. And when you do need to charge it, there's support for up to 33W wired fast charging.

Of course, there are a few compromises at this price. The tablet is powered by the MediaTek Helio G100 chipset, which isn't exactly a flagship processor. It's perfectly reasonable for everyday tasks like reading, browsing, and streaming, but don't expect the same performance you'd get from a more flagship Samsung Galaxy tablet or iPad.

That remarked, if you're looking for a relatively inexpensive tablet this Black Friday that also doubles as an e-reader, this is probably one of the best deals you can get right now.
